title: Why Bengaluru Floods Every Single Monsoon
creator: The Civic Explainer
description:
Every year the same roads go under water. We look at the lakes that disappeared, the drains that were built over, and what the city is actually doing about it.

0:00 The night the Outer Ring Road flooded
1:10 A city built on lakes
2:45 Where the water used to go
4:00 What can fix it

sentences.t: Last September I was stuck on the Outer Ring Road for almost four hours.
Not in traffic, exactly, in water, the road had just become a river.
There were cars with water up to the doors, there were people wading with their shoes in their hands.
And my phone, a very old OnePlus that I really should have replaced years ago, died at about the second hour.
So I couldn't even call home, I just sat there watching the auto in front of me slowly float sideways.
And the thing that bothered me the most was that nobody around me was surprised.
Everyone was annoyed, sure, but nobody was shocked, because this happens every year.
So today we're asking a simple question, why does Bengaluru flood every single monsoon?
To understand that, you have to know that this city was basically designed around lakes.
Starting in the sixteenth century, local rulers built hundreds of tanks, artificial lakes, connected to each other in chains.
Rain would fill the highest lake, it would overflow into a channel, and that channel would fill the next lake down.
These channels are called rajakaluves, and they're the key to this whole story.
It was a brilliant system for a dry city, you caught every drop of rain and you stored it.
In the 1960s, by some estimates, there were well over two hundred lakes within the city.
Today a big chunk of those are gone, or so shrunk and polluted you'd barely call them lakes.
So where did they go?
Some became bus stands, some became stadiums, some became entire neighborhoods.
One of the city's biggest bus terminals literally sits on a lake that used to be there.
And when the lakes went, the channels between them mostly went too.
They got narrowed, or covered with concrete, or built over completely, sometimes by apartments, sometimes by tech parks.
So now imagine the rain comes, the same heavy monsoon rain that's always come.
It runs downhill, the way water always has, looking for the channel that used to carry it to the next lake.
And the channel isn't there, or it's a quarter of its old width, or it's choked with plastic and construction waste.
So the water goes where it can, which is the road, and the basement parking, and the ground floor of your building.
And it's not just lost lakes, the whole city is more concrete than it used to be.
Rain that used to soak into soil now hits tarmac and rooftops and runs straight off.
Some studies estimate the built-up area of the city grew by more than a thousand percent over a few decades.
So you've got more water running off, and fewer places for it to go, which is basically the recipe for what I sat in last September.
Okay, so what can actually fix it?
The city has been clearing encroachments on the drains, and to be fair, some big buildings have had parts demolished.
But it's slow, and it's very political, because a lot of those encroachments belong to people with money and influence.
The other piece is restoring lakes, and there are some genuine success stories here, often led by local residents.
Neighborhood groups have cleaned up lakes, fixed the inlets, and got the water flowing again.
And honestly, those projects are the most hopeful thing I found while researching this video.
Because the old system wasn't broken, it was just paved over, and parts of it can be brought back.
Let us know in the comments if your area floods, and which roads, because we want to map it for a follow-up.
Thanks for watching, and stay dry out there.
